and sameness within and without.
If one discusses this in terms of the house:
that which the various conditions share with the house as a whole is "superior sameness" (ūrdhva-samatā);
that which the house as a whole shares with the various conditions is "inferior sameness" (adhaḥ-samatā).
Regarding the aforementioned "internal similarity" (*antarasādharmya*): when various conditions are similar within a house, this is internal similarity.
When various conditions, in relation to one another, possess an equal capacity to constitute a house, this is external similarity (*bahirdhāsādharmya*).
Furthermore, there are two meanings: partial correspondence (*bhāga-sama*) and total correspondence (*pūrṇa-sama*).
This means that when a single foot of tile exerts the same amount of effort as twenty paces of a hall, it is "partial correspondence.
When a single foot of tile exerts the same amount of effort as twenty paces of a hall, it is "total correspondence."

"Distinct characteristics" (vilakṣaṇa) indicates the meaning that the various conditions which can bring about formation possess distinct forms and types, each remaining immovable in its respective position. Question:
If they were truly distinct, [how could they function together]?
Should they not be identical? Answer:
It is precisely because of their difference that the sense of identity can exist.
If they were not different, [identity would be impossible].
If the roof tiles are one chi and the rafters are also one chi,
they deviate from their original causal positions and lose the prior sense of uniformity required for constructing a house.
Question: If that were so, and a single foot-long tile produced the same force as a hall twenty paces long upon being cast twenty paces away,
and the same applied to rafters,
would this not also constitute a loss of the original causal status?
Answer: If a tile moves from its position of one chi, it is equivalent to a rafter moving from its position of twelve chi;
only then does it exert a force of twenty paces.
The same applies to the rafter.
They ought to lose their original positions;
yet the tile does not move from its original position of one chi,
nor does the rafter move from its position of twelve zhang.
Yet, because each exerts its own strength of twenty paces and they are equal in their hall,
although both exert the same strength of twenty paces, the tile is not a ten-foot beam and the beam is not a one-foot tile;
since each remains in its own position, there is no contradiction.
Regarding the characteristic of accomplishment (*siddha-lakṣaṇa*): it clarifies the non-acting of acting;
that is to say, because each of the various conditions remains unmoving in its respective position, the state of equanimity (*upekṣā*) is accomplished.
In the preceding section on common characteristics,
it was shown that the various conditions, such as the rafters and so forth, possess an equal capacity for the power of forming the house when they are mutually related and mutually inclusive.
Furthermore, this is established with reference to the rafters and all other such conditions.
From the perspective of the whole, the rafters are supported by the ridge-pole;
from the perspective of the eaves, the rafters support the house.
Thus, there is the principle of mutual orientation, mutual inclusion, and mutual support.
Within this characteristic of accomplishment,
according to any single condition,
it is precisely the absolute totality that is free from dependence and partiality.
That which is capable of acting as a condition has nothing else to be produced externally;
therefore, the principle of mutual inclusion is not mentioned in relation to them. As for the characteristic of disintegration:
"Clarifying non-action within action" means that various conditions, such as rafters and so forth, each abide in their own nature, fundamentally unmoving. Question:
What is the distinction between this "non-movement" and the "non-movement" mentioned previously among the diverse characteristics?
Answer: Because their positions do not shift within the previously mentioned distinct characteristics.
Although the one-foot position of a tile and the ten-foot position of a rafter each remain stationary, they possess the sense of being in relation to one another.
In this context, because their essence is immovable,
phenomena do not cognize one another; this is explained according to the hall of established characteristics.
Is it established by means of the pillars among those conditions? Or even by the tiles?
Thus, when interrogated exhaustively, not a single thing is found that establishes that hall.
By means of this, the ultimate realization of the Hall of Characteristics is accomplished;
for it is through non-action that action is performed, and thus the characteristic of destruction itself becomes accomplishment.
This is not a destruction that involves annihilation.
An ancient record states:
It was asked of an ancient master: [What is this?]
The Hall of Causes and Conditions succeeds when it is constructed;
it does not succeed when it is not constructed.
The Hall of Dependent Origination does not succeed even when it is constructed.
If one does not act, then accomplishment is attained.
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is: it is the same as the house of non-action within the house of action.

This is because the characteristic of completion (siddha-lakṣaṇa) relinquishes the activity of non-action (anabhisamskāra). When the characteristic of sameness (sādhāraṇa-lakṣaṇa) and the characteristic of completion are explained in relation to one another,
the characteristic of sameness refers to the meaning of the manifestation of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda).
The characteristic of formation is the meaning of dependent origination being devoid of intrinsic nature.
It is explained in contrast to the characteristic of disintegration;
thus, the characteristic of formation is so called because it does not act as an agent.
The meaning of dependent origination as being without intrinsic nature:
because that which possesses characteristics is neither produced nor unproduced,
this is the meaning of dependent origination as being without intrinsic nature.
An ancient verse says:
"Beginning from the stone at the base of the pillar and ending with the tiles atop the beams—this is the Hall of Universal Imputation (parikalpita) for establishing the entire house.
Carrying the axe to strike the wood, and with each successive blow establishing the entire house—this is the Hall of Dependent Origination (paratantra)."
When the axe does not fall upon the wood and the wood does not come into contact with the axe, that which stands complete is the Hall of Dependent Origination (Pratītyasamutpāda).
When the wood-sprouts are green, that which stands complete is the Hall of Essential Origination (Svabhāvodaya).
Within this Essential Origination, there is...
When planting the tree-seed, it establishes the entire hall; there is no separate dwelling hall.
The seed itself is the true reality, which is the Hall of Real Mark (Skt.
*dharmatā*). K'ang-tsang said:
What is the house? The rafters themselves are the house. Why is this so?
Because it is asked: "If a single rafter were entirely capable of constructing a house by itself," and so forth.
"Even when tiles and such are not yet present, one should still be able to build a house.
Answer: "When tiles and such are not yet present, they do not constitute rafters; therefore, [the structure] does not abide as a house.
Question: "Even though tiles and such are absent..."
We clearly see this rafter;
why do you say that it is not a rafter when there are no tiles? [The opponent] replies:
This is merely a difficulty raised by way of parikalpa (conceptual construction).
The Great Sūtra says:
"The ocean of wisdom is vast and boundless; those who fail to fathom it only increase their slander.
How can one not be cautious? Do not, O Mother, harbor a mind subject to arising and ceasing."
One may doubt the principle of the true reality;
yet this rafter of the causal conditions of my universal Dharma,
being a single rafter, inherently encompasses all other rafters of its own kind.
Whether it be a one-foot bracket-arch,
an eight-foot pillar,
or even down to the roof tiles and stones.
The carpenter who fashions the timber and the potter who fires the tiles—
these and all other dharmas are universally and exhaustively gathered to bring the construction of the house to completion;
only then can they be called rafters.
It is for this reason that you say so.

An ancient said: "To gather pillars today with the intent of building a house already completed yesterday—if that were so, would the house already completed yesterday have been built without pillars?"

Since it is said that one gathers pillars today with the intent of building a house already completed yesterday, we know that the house already completed yesterday was not formed without pillars. The above.
Therefore, it is only when the house is completed that it is a pillar;
likewise, it is only when the house is completed that it is a rafter.
The *Zhēnjì* states:
Regarding what are called the six characteristics:
the general purport here is that Rocana Buddha is the most honored and supreme.
We sentient beings are the most inferior.
Śānta is the general characteristic (sāmānyalakṣaṇa);
"sentient beings" is the specific characteristic (viśeṣalakṣaṇa).
The bodies of sentient beings have no separate self-nature;
they are entirely formed from the body of Śākyamuni.
Nevertheless, for the present, the two are shown to have distinct meanings.
Because it is not other, it is said to be non-arising;
because it is not one, it is said to arise.
Thus, K'ang-tsang said:
Regarding the fact that the derivative does not arise or cease apart from the fundamental:
as for their identical nature, it is because, with respect to the bodies of sentient beings, there is no other substance whatsoever; they are exclusively the Buddha-body.
Regarding the fact that the bodies of sentient beings carry that Buddha yet possess different characteristics:
although the bodies of sentient beings carry the body of that Buddha, [they appear otherwise].
While it is immovable, it is able to carry sentient beings eternally.
In terms of the sense of "carrying," there is similarity;
in terms of the sense of "sentient beings," there is difference.
Therefore, the Kang-tsang says:
"Since that which arises as the derivative (the end) already carries the fundamental (the root),
when they are compared with one another, there are both similarities and differences."
Regarding the characteristic of accomplishment:
the bodies of inferior sentient beings are themselves the bodies of the sublime and honored Buddhas;
there is not even a hair’s breadth of difference between them at any time.
Therefore, one does not cause [the contemplation] to be identical to that;
for while the contemplation of common characteristics causes it to be identical to that,
the contemplation of perfected characteristics is simply the One Reality itself.
Regarding the characteristic of disintegration: the various phenomena that differentiate the dharma-realm each remain unmoving;
this is precisely the nature of the true, functional virtue within the bodies of sentient beings, abiding in the Middle Way.
It is simply the One True Reality.
Therefore, it is said that "existence" persists;
yet because each [aspect] remains unmoving within itself, it is also said that "destruction" exists.
Therefore, the Kangzang (Kongtrul) said:
"Since that which is the end of the fundamental [nature] is already subsumed within the fundamental,
it follows that the essence itself both exists and undergoes destruction."
An ancient record states:
Formerly, Rin-chen-grags (Rinde) entered Tang China to pose difficult questions to the masters Jñānamitra (Jung) and Śīlabhadra (Sun). He asked:
"Once one has already attained Buddhahood, why does one not initially move from the ordinary body?"
Shun said: "Among the six characteristics, there is both identity and difference.
What difficulty is there in this? End of quote.
Question: Why is it not stated that there are six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), but instead only the "same" and "different" are specifically singled out?
Answer: If one speaks in terms of the house as being distinct.
Thus, the rafters and other conditions are merely distinct from the house as a whole;
it does not mean that one perceives their curved shapes or long and short dimensions.
Furthermore, when they are destroyed, one simply sees the various conditions each abiding in their own dharmas, having originally performed no action at all.
Only the characteristics of similarity and difference, when coordinated according to a single condition, encompass and integrate all conditions to fulfill the functional meaning of a complete house;
yet while the pillars are eight feet high,
the rafters are twelve feet long.
The tiles are over a foot in length;
because these various positions of differing lengths each remain unmoving,
one should simply grasp this principle and provide the answer.
The Chapter on the Six Characteristics states:
"One is identical with the possession of many names; this is the general characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa). Many are not one; this is the particular characteristic (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa)."
Many categories, being identical in nature, constitute a totality;
each individual essence, though distinct, manifests as the same.
The principle of the dependent origination of the one and the many is subtle and wondrous.
The formation, destruction, and abiding of phenomena do not arise from their own nature;
they are the domain of wisdom alone, not of the consciousness of phenomenal objects.
By this expedient means, one realizes the One Vehicle.
The *Mahā-tantra* states:

"The general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) is the fundamental seal (*mūla-mudrā*); the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) consists of the other seals of various curved forms and their respective bases.
'Because it fulfills those seals' means..."
The root seal (mūdrā) is the general [principle] that transcends particulars;
the seal of fulfillment is the general [principle] that encompasses particulars.
Although there are these two meanings, [they are one].
Yet there is no duality of the universal;
that which is called "universal" has no particularity to correspond to it.
Therefore, it is said to be "free from particulars."
However, since this general category of "separation" is formed by encompassing its particulars,
it is said to "include the particulars.
One opens up the particulars based upon the general.
There are both the "separated" and the "fully opened.
Therefore, with respect to the meaning of being fully opened, it is called "filling that mudrā.
Question: If that is so, would there not be no further fundamental totality apart from these?
Why is it said that there are "relying on seals" (*yīn yìn*) and "fulfilling seals" (*mǎn yìn*)?
Answer: Speaking from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), one should not speak of "relying on seals" or "fulfilling seals."

However, because one wishes to cause [them] to understand that there is no partiality and that they do not reach a state of mutual cognition, it is said that the capacity and the object are fully present in this way. Regarding the "common characteristic" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) as being "seal-like" (mudrā):
although each of the various curves and so forth is distinct, [they share this commonality].
This is because they are equally circular seals.
"Equally" has two meanings:
namely, they are equal, and thus identical.
They are identical because they are one.
They are identical because they are equal:
this refers to the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) among the six aspects as presented in the sequential gates.
The power and meaning of all conditions are equal when they are viewed in relation to one another.
As for "being the same because they are one":
the common characteristic (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) is subsumed within a single condition; thus, all conditions are collectively grasped as a whole.
Regarding the phrase "as for 'having different characteristics,' it is because they increase":
this means that the initial bend and the subsequent bends each differ by an increasing number.
There are two senses in which there is an "increase."
This refers to internal increase and external increase. That is to say,
when the various conditions of the aggregate are not mutually consistent, it is internal increase.
When the various conditions that mutually face one another and harmoniously penetrate are not identical, they increase toward the external.
As for the phrase "the characteristics of formation are explained briefly," it means that various curved lines combine to form a single seal.
As for the point at which all conditions reach their ultimate limit, it is said that "a single condition" is precisely the totality; therefore, it is called a "brief explanation.
As for the phrase "the characteristic of disintegration is an extensive explanation," it means:
Each of the various verses abides in its own fundamental state because they are not produced through effort;
by universally examining all conditions so that they reach a state of neither increase nor decrease, they remain as they naturally are.
Therefore, it is called "extensive exposition."
The *Faji* states:
"The general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is the fundamental seal; the specific characteristics (*viśeṣalakṣaṇa*) are the others, which are tortuous.
Generally, the one contains many virtues."
In other words, there are many virtues rather than just one.
Question: What is this "one," and what are these "many virtues"?
Answer: The meaning of the Dharma-realm as being "one" without partiality toward any particular phenomenon is one;
the meaning of this "one without partiality" being inexhaustible is its manifold virtues.
Question: How is the meaning of this "one without partiality" being inexhaustible to be perceived?
The answer is: for the time being, it is said that these conditions collectively constitute one hall;
this means that each and every condition individually fulfills the hall.
That is to say, whichever single dharma is raised, it is complete in itself without requiring anything else to arise alongside it.
That which is absolute and independent is the one without counterpart.
The distinct virtues contained within this one also each encompass and unify every single ultimate reality.
Therefore, each and every condition is fully complete as the Dharma.
This is the virtue of inexhaustibility.
To speak by way of analogy:
the spiritual friend Mañjuśrī is wisdom that illuminates the non-dual nature.
If one were to explain this according to its various bases,
then when Sudhana saw Mañjuśrī,
he would have seen as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in the three thousandfold world system.
This means that because the illuminating wisdom and the illuminated object are one and the same,
when one perceives a single Mañjuśrī,
the three thousandfold world-system upon which he relies is itself consciousness.
Therefore, it is said that one immediately perceives as many spiritual teachers (jñānin) as there are atoms in the three thousandfold world system.
If one speaks from the perspective of relinquishing the basis upon which they depend,
then all phenomena within the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) are subsumed to become a single Mañjuśrī.
When one sees a single Mañjuśrī,
one not only gains the vision of as many spiritual friends as there are atoms in three thousandfold worlds,
but also immediately encounters as many virtuous friends as there are atoms in the entire Dharma-realm.

Therefore, according to a single Mañjuśrī, there are as many spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) as there are atoms in the three thousandfold world-system reaching to the limits of the Dharma-realm, and each one of them likewise reaches to the limits of the Dharma-realm.
Question: If that is so, then is it one Mañjuśrī?
"Many Mañjuśrīs? He replied, "According to how they are designated, they are one Mañjuśrī;
according to how they are designated, they are one hall."
Therefore, it is possible for there to be one Mañjuśrī,
and it is also possible for there to be many Mañjuśrīs;
it is possible for them to be in a single hall as well.
It is also acceptable to have many halls.
Regarding "the same characteristic being the seal":
this means that the fifty-four corners are identical because they form a single circular seal.
It is said that although they differ in form, they share the same seal (*mudrā*).
Question: What is the meaning of "partial sameness" (*bun-dō*) and "complete sameness" (*man-dō*)?
Answer: It is impossible to divide the great void (*mahā-ākāśa*), yet it is divided into the ten directions.
On the other hand, when space is identical to the great void,
the spaces of the ten directions are simultaneously identical; they are identical in their fullness.
To see similarity only in one direction while not seeing similarity in other directions is partial similarity.
Regarding the phrase "the distinct characteristic is because it is an increasing characteristic":
does this refer to an increase in number,
or an increase in stage?
The answer states: First,
it is said that because one counts from the first corner to the second corner in this manner,
as the number increases, the position likewise increases.
One interpretation states:
because they are counted as "first" and "second," it is called an increase in number;
however, it is not an increase in horns.
It is not an increase in status.
As for the phrase "because the characteristics of accomplishment are explained briefly," it is,
for example, like a person standing in front of a hall.
Just as when a person calls out to the assembly within the hall with a single word and the assembly all respond verbally,
so it is when one calls upon the seal with a single word.
Since all fifty-four corners are themselves seals (*mudrā*),
Kāṅ-tsang says: "The harmony and conjunction of conditions are briefly expressed and manifested."
Question: In the section on "common characteristics" (*sādharmya*), it was explained that each individual corner is identical to the circular seal.
What is the meaning clarified here?
Answer: It means that the curvature of each individual corner is itself the seal; this is merely for the sake of establishing the characteristic of completion.
It does not mean that the various horns constitute the seal.
Regarding the phrase "because the characteristics are extensively explained," it is like taking a human body and interrogating the person's name.
There is not a single corner that receives the name "round seal.
Thus, having extensively analyzed them in sequence, one refutes all fifty-four corners;
for there is not a single corner that receives the name "round seal."
Kangtsang said:
"The phrase 'the dispersal of conditions and non-action' extensively elucidates causes and conditions.
Therefore, this is the most perfect among all seals."
This is the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
As for the curved corners of the seals of the *paripūrṇamudrā*,
these are the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).
When the two corners of the curves are aligned and identical in their seal,
this is the mark of sameness. When they are aligned and identical in their seal yet remain unmoving and distinct from one another, this is the mark of difference.
This is the characteristic of differentiation.
That which is immovable yet not biased toward any particularity, being the very seal of correctness,
is the characteristic of fulfillment.
That which is precisely the seal yet each abides in itself without acting as a creator—
this is the characteristic of destruction.
This gateway of the six characteristics is precisely the unique expedient means of the One Vehicle.
This is also the essence of the unshared dharmas (*āveṇika-dharma*). Using these six characteristics to temporarily align them with the three contemplations:

the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) corresponds to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*); while similarity and difference correspond to the contemplation of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).

The contemplation of arising and ceasing is the contemplation of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); the fundamental totality is the contemplation of the manifestation of nature (dharmatā-prakṛti).
These are merely expressions made by way of provisional stages.
If one considers this from the perspective of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna),
then there is no difference in depth between the three contemplations of causes and conditions, dependent origination, and the arising of nature.

That which pertains to general characteristics corresponds in meaning to the Perfect Teaching (Vendantā-yāna), while that which pertains to specific characteristics corresponds in meaning to the teachings of the Three Vehicles.
Question: Is the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) the same as the Common Teaching (tongjiao), or is it the Distinct Teaching (biejiao)?
Answer: It is the Common Teaching.
That is to say, the seal being circular signifies the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao),
while the fifty-four corners signify the Three Vehicles (Sanche).
Therefore, both the Perfect Teaching and the Three Vehicles are of the same teaching (Tongjiao).
Why is this? Because apart from the seal there is no circle,
and apart from the corners there is no seal-circle.
The *Daji* (Great Record) states:
Linde established five levels of general and specific categories based on this location, namely:
first, the general category of separation.
This is the primary "Ocean Seal" (Sāgaramudrā) among the five layers of ocean seals.
It is the totality that encompasses particulars while remaining distinct from them;
it is also called the totality that manifests within conditions while remaining distinct from those conditions.
This is the second ocean-seal.
Third, the general is the particular, and the particular is the general;
this is the third ocean-seal.
The fourth is both general and specific;
this is the fourth sea-seal.
The fifth is neither general nor specific.
This is the fifth ocean-seal (sāgara-mudrā).
It is said that because it gathers particulars to form a whole, it is not a whole;
and because it relies on the whole to form particulars, it is not a particular.
This is because they are simultaneously eclipsed by one another. Within these five layers,
the first is general and the subsequent ones are specific.
Furthermore, the second is general while the third is specific;
thus they are designated as general and specific in relation to one another.
Moreover, each of these two also possesses its own general and specific aspects.
That is to say, excluding the first Sea-Seal [Samādhi],
within the second layer,
the Buddha’s realized mind is the totality.
The distinctions manifested within the three worlds are no less significant than the totality itself; herein,
there is neither identity nor difference, neither formation nor destruction.
Because this totality and its particulars are of one essence,
they constitute the true source into which the six aspects of dependent origination enter.
This occurs at the third level.
It is not that the six aspects (ṣaḷlakṣaṇa) are not employed;
rather, these are the six aspects of the essence of the Dharma itself, not those of the provisional means.
They are to be correlated starting from the fourth stage onward.
The three contemplations—causality (*hetu-pratyaya*), dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), and the nature of arising (*svabhāva-utpāda*)—contain three meanings.
Namely: first, the general characteristic refers to the non-abiding distinct teachings;
second, the specific characteristics refer to the three vehicles that flow from them.
Regarding the objects of observation:
the contemplation of causes and conditions concerns the characteristics of identity and difference;
the contemplation of dependent origination concerns the characteristic of formation.
The characteristic of destruction is the contemplation of the arising of nature (*dharmatā-utpatti*).
Herein, it is distinguished as a "distinct characteristic" (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) only in reference to the disease to be remedied;
it is not a distinct characteristic among the six characteristics of the remedy itself.
Second, setting aside the non-abiding distinct teaching and the distinct adherence to the three vehicles,
regarding the categories within the objective realm,
as for the characteristics of the general and the specific, there is the Contemplation of Nature-Arising (xingqi).

The characteristic of identity and difference is the contemplation of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*); the characteristic of formation and destruction is the contemplation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, each of these three contemplations individually possesses the six characteristics.
This fourth layer and beyond constitute the six aspects of skillful means (*upāya*).
It is through these five layers that the meaning and principles of the various passages are fully exhausted;
this present text contains all five layers.
An ancient record states that on the eleventh day of the tenth month in the first year of the Zongzhang era,
Master Xiang questioned Master Yan at the Prajñā Hall of Qingchan Temple.
Regarding the ritual procedure for upholding the Universal Dharma,
the Master asked:
"Are you able to uphold it?"
Furthermore, "lifting the collar hair" means to align the general principles with the specific details; this is correctness.
A question was asked: "What is the meaning of this?
The Master said:
Down to the mundane dharmas,
all are the Middle Way and the true aspect (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
He then expounded ten layers of general and specific categories to demonstrate this.
The text concerning the general and the particular in Master Yan’s *Xinglu* (Record of Practice) is precisely this.
First, there is conformity with the general and divergence from the particular;
that is to say, because the dharmas of the general characteristics as fruits are established through conditions as numerous as atoms.
If it is in accordance [with the principle], it is "comprehensive" (zong), because it establishes the comprehensive by taking the particular as its object;
if it is contrary, it is "particular" (bie).
Second, "contradicting the general while conforming to the particular.
This means that because the conditions that establish the general remain immobile within their own state, they contradict [the general];
thus, it is "general" [in its contradiction].
Because they can be accomplished while remaining unmoved from their own positions;
thus, in accordance with this, the particular is the general, and the general is the particular of the particular.
This means that because the particular is entirely the universal, the universal is like the particular;
and because the universal is entirely the particular, the particular is like the universal.
Fourth, there is the universal that the particular does not know, and the particular that the universal does not know.
This means that because there is no distinct aspect within the whole that is being established, the particular does not know the whole;
and because there is no aspect of a whole within the conditions that establish it, the whole does not know the particular.
The fifth is the "totality of separation" and the "separation from totality.
This means that within the fruit of the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because there is nothing that is not encompassed by conditions, it is the "totality of separation";
and because there is no distinction between the totality and its particulars, it is the "separation from totality."
The six types of non-abiding consist of both the general and the specific.
"Non-abiding" means the sense of lacking self-mastery.
Because the dharmas that are results, by their general characteristic, do not abide in themselves, they are called the "general non-abiding."
This non-abiding is the general [aspect], because among conditions as numerous as atoms, there is nothing to which it is specifically attached; thus it is the particular [aspect] of non-abiding.
Seventh, the real mark (lakṣaṇa) is both general and particular.
That is to say, the general aspect refers to the fruit-dharmas, which are the realization of knowing that is free from the conceptual discrimination of wisdom; thus it is the general real mark.
Because conditions have no distinct characteristics, their true nature is distinct;
that is to say, it is "signlessness" (animitta).
The nature of the eight dharmas is the general nature of all dharmas.
This means that because the nature of dharmas as universal characteristics (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) is inherently pervasive and harmonious, when encountering conditions, it accords with them;
thus, the nature of dharmas is universal. Since this accordant dharma arises entirely and without partiality, it is called the "nature of dharmas" (dharma-prakṛti).
The nine [aspects] consist of the general seal of the ocean and the specific seals of the ocean.
This means that because the inexhaustible categories of dharmas manifest all at once in their entirety without omission, it is called the "general seal of the ocean.
Because the dharmas manifested all at once do not cognize one another, it is called the "specific seal of the ocean."
The ten proofs consist of both general and specific proofs.
This means that because the fruit-dharmas of general characteristics are realized only by a Buddha, they are called "general proofs.
Within these realizations, because all dharmas are immovable, they are called "specific proofs."
Lindeyun said:

"Only after employing these ten types of methods for synthesizing the general and the particular can one finally perceive that a single speck of dust, a single ant, and Śākyamuni Buddha are fundamentally one and the same body."
Based on such meanings as these, there then exist the simultaneous fulfillment and the subtle realm of Indra’s net. Question:
What is the difference between the fourth [section], the general and specific, and the fifth?
Answer: Although the fourth layer does not involve mutual cognition, it is not that there is no distinction between the two positions.
As for the fifth layer, it is "distinct" because it speaks of the "total" and the "particular" with respect to a single entity.
Question: What is the difference between the general and specific aspects of the sixth [category], Non-abiding, and the general and specific aspects of the seventh, True Reality (dharmatā)?
Answer: Since True Reality is said to be "free from the conceptualization of cognition," it distinguishes itself from the cognition of the sixth, Non-abiding.
As for the eighth [point], it can be understood that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is fully endowed with both principle and wisdom.
The *Dajiji* states:
"From the general characteristics and specific characteristics, up to the fact that they always abide in the Middle Way."
There are two interpretations.
One holds that the word "as" (yathā) is spoken only after proceeding from the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) to the middle way.
The other holds that the word "as" is spoken immediately following both the general characteristic and the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*).
The commentary explains:

According to the first sense, the particular is not the general, and the general is not established as the particular; thus, non-destruction is not establishment, and destruction is not establishment, and so forth.
Therefore, it is said that they are neither identical nor different.
However, because the whole is entirely contained within each part and each part is entirely contained within the whole,
it is said that they are neither separate nor different.
According to the latter sense, "neither identical nor separate" refers to the characteristics of formation and destruction.
"Neither identical nor different" refers to the characteristics of identity and difference.
This means that when teaching those below [the stage of realization] up to the point of the ultimate fruit,
one clings to the notion that the true and the delusive share the same essence.
By sealing it with the seal of the mark of destruction,
the true and the false each abide in their original state without movement; therefore,
it is said they are "not identical."
Seal it with the seal of the characteristic of fulfillment;
thus, the true and the false are one with the true.
Therefore, it is said that they are not separate.
Furthermore, because there is the affliction of perceiving a distinction between ordinary beings and sages at the stage where initial awakening (shikaku) coincides with original awakening (hongaku),
one treats this by means of the aspect of sameness (dōsō).
That is to say, by means of the sun of original awakening itself, one realizes that the bodies of ordinary beings and sages are one and the same.
One treats it with the aspect of difference,
for since ordinary beings and sages are each distinct, they are said to be not one.
One treats it with the aspect of sameness.
Because the measure of both ordinary beings and sages is one and the same, it is said that they are not different.
Thus, by means of the three contemplations— such as those of causes and conditions, dependent origination, and so forth—
one counteracts the maladies of the three vehicles' distinct attachments to identity and difference, or their separation from them.
The retinues of the three vehicles and the Lord of the One Vehicle are companions who are neither identical nor separate;
thus they constitute a Lord and Retinue that are perfectly luminous and endowed with all virtues.
Question: If one employs the six characteristics (*ṣaḷlakṣaṇa*), the afflictions should already be exhausted.
Why is it necessary to further employ the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)?
Answer: If one attains the general characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the four propositions are not required.
However, this is merely stated as four propositions for the sake of those who hold different views.
Regarding the mutual formation of the primary and secondary aspects of the One Vehicle and the Three Vehicles:
one asks, "Is the One Vehicle exclusively the primary and the Three Vehicles the secondary?"
Or is it the opposite? Answer: Some say that although it is as stated below, [it is nonetheless so].
It is solely the single, exclusive One Vehicle that is the primary, while the Three Vehicles are its attendants.
That is to say, the single, exclusive entry into the fundamental [reality] is termed "general," whereas the nine entries are termed "particular" only.
It is not that the name "entry by means of the root" is designated as distinct;
rather, because the remaining nine entries are designated as general,
it is solely the name "One Vehicle" that serves as the general and primary designation.
The names of the three vehicles are designated as distinct yet mutually supportive.
Question: If this is so, why is it said that the primary and the supportive are established in mutual dependence?
Answer: It is because of the One Vehicle that there are three vehicles.
Because of the three vehicles, there is the one vehicle;
therefore, the one vehicle subsumes the three vehicles as its primary essence,
while the three vehicles depend upon the one vehicle as their companion.
Therefore, it is said that they "mutually establish" one another.

As for the statement that "the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle and the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles can be understood by analogy," this is because the application of the principle of the six characteristics pertains exclusively to the gates of the identical teaching.
Excluding the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle and the distinct teachings of the Three Vehicles,
if one were to explain in detail,
the distinct teaching of the One Vehicle would be primary.
The distinct teachings of the three vehicles are its retinue and companions;
based on these, the meaning of the manifestation of the Middle Way can be understood by analogy. One says:
It was stated previously that both the Perfect Teaching and the Three Vehicles are all of the same teaching (tóngjiào).
Now, this One Vehicle distinct teaching (biéjiào) is profound compared to the same teaching,
whereas the distinct teaching of the Three Vehicles is shallow compared to the same teaching.
This can be understood by analogy with the meaning.
The *Faji* (Record of the Dharma) states:
"Only those who abide in their own suchness."
This is not the equality of True Suchness in which the three vehicles are fused in appearance while their essence remains unfused;

rather, it refers to the state where both essence and appearance are fused and non-discriminatory, wherein, within the destruction of appearances, there is from the outset no sense of things abiding separately as they are.
Regarding the statement that "the levels differ because they rely on the provisional teaching gates of the three vehicles":
if one considers the practice according to the three vehicles' provisional teachings,
then the sequential arrangement of cause and effect results in different levels of high and low.
If one follows the true intent of the One Vehicle, then cause and effect are perfectly interfused; the virtuous functions of the dharma-nature reside solely within the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is said that there is no sequence of before and after.
The *Jianyi zhang* (Chapter on the Meaning of Simplification) states:
"The teaching of the harmonious fusion and sequential arrangement has four gates:
first, the sequential arrangement of the Three Vehicles and the harmonious fusion of the One Vehicle."
As the text states:
"Because they rely on the provisional teaching gates of the Three Vehicles, there are differences in high and low;
because they rely on the perfect teaching of the One Vehicle, there is no sequence of before and after."
Second, within this sutra,
there are two types of external common teachings:
first, the superior commonality.
Drawing in space toward space is identical in essence to space itself; accordingly, it is unimpeded in every respect.
The same applies to the second [case].
The following is like drawing on earth, for there is a distinction between before and after.
The former [the upper part] is the meaning of perfect interfusion;
the latter [the lower part] is the meaning of sequential arrangement.
This is because, as in the "Earth" chapter, a single bird's footprint is made to pervade both.
The three external aspects of the Shared Teaching (sāmānya-dharma) constitute the sequential arrangement (vyavasthāna),
while the intrinsic nature of the Distinct Teaching (pratyeka-dharma) constitutes the perfect fusion (yuanrong).
As stated in the *Suoshuǎn-zhāng*:
Regarding the establishment of the various teachings, there are two types of skillfulness, and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Kejian* (Excerpts) states:
"The stage of Samantabhadra has two types," which refers to this.
Fourth, regarding the distinct teaching according to their own essence:
that which does not disrupt its original position is the sequential (xingbu),
and that which is unimpeded and perfectly interfused is the circular (yuanrong).
That is to say: it is divided into the extensive, the narrow, and the intermediate, yet remains undivided;
furthermore, while entering the gates of characteristics, its lack of intrinsic nature is indestructible;
moreover, without moving from its own station, it is constantly coming and going.
Furthermore, among the six characteristics, there are the three aspects of perfect fusion and the three aspects of sequential arrangement,
and so forth. Regarding all bodhisattvas reaching [the realization of] the aggregates, elements, sense bases,
and so on, the *Fajiji* states:
The Commentary states: "All bodhisattvas" refers to those dwelling on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhā-caryā-bhūmi*).
"Faith" refers to the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*); "practice" refers to the three stages of worthiness (*tri-pṛthagjana-kula*).
"Bhūmi" refers to the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
If categorized according to the major divisions,
the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*) consists of the three levels of worthiness (*trayaḥ kalyāṇamitras*).
That which is realized is the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
The inconceivable qualities of the Buddha-dharma are the supramundane factors of enlightenment (*lokottara-bodhipakṣa-dharma*).
These inconceivable Buddha-dharmas are precisely the internal realization of the Buddha.
This means that it is like a pond of water containing reflections;
there are two senses involved:
namely, the sense of encompassing all reflected images.
Furthermore, when various reflected images appear,
suppose there is a person standing by the side of the pond who sees these images and describes them to others.
In this way, the Buddha realizes the threefold world as his own body and mind,
just as various images are reflected within water.
Through his internal realization, he outwardly manifests the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) according to the needs of the occasion.

Just as various images appear within water, so too did Vajragarbha, while in meditative absorption, receive the Buddha’s teaching on the outward-directed Dharma; having emerged from that concentration, he then expounded it for the sake of those with the appropriate capacity.
It is like that one person standing by the edge of a pond who sees the reflection in the water and describes it to others;
that is to say, from the perspective of internal realization,
there is only the inconceivable Dharma.
There is no characteristic of the ten stages;
however, because the capacities of those previously encountered were mostly of the three vehicles,
the Buddha intended to cause them to be taught the ten stages.
Therefore, within the outward-directed mind, the ten stages (daśabhūmi) are provisionally indicated.
This meaning is vast and ineffable.
It is after Vajragarbha has entered meditative absorption, received this Dharma, and emerged from that concentration that he speaks of the ten stages.
This is what is called "the great that can be spoken. Thus Zhixiang said:
"The stages (bhūmi) have two divisions."
There are one cause and two fruits.
The cause refers to the cultivation of worldly expedient practices;
that is, the stage of preparatory application (*prayoga-bhūmi*).
"Result" refers to supramundane, signless true realization;
it is the very extent of the wisdom of correct realization.
As for the "supramundane factors of enlightenment":
Question: For what reason are there factors of the path (mārga-aṅga) in the supramundane state?
Answer: If one considers it from the perspective of inconceivable dharmas, then although there are no factors of the path, [they are nonetheless present].
Nevertheless, because the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are provisionally revealed according to the capacities and conditions of sentient beings, there is the section on the "Path" (*mārga-varga*).
Therefore, Zhizhi (Zhìxiàng) states:
"These present ten stages encompass the causal stage of the Buddha."
The One Vehicle, the Three Vehicles, śrāvakas, humans, and devas are all contained therein;
it is that which is contemplated by the five vehicles.
Samantabhadra’s stage of realization is subsumed within the fruit of Buddhahood, wherein functions are unimpeded and sovereign.
All are exhausted. Why is this?
Because the Dharma of the Ten Stages is the primary gateway for encompassing sentient beings.
This is because the dharmas of the stages are extremely profound and most difficult to discern.
Those who are wise, who see with knowledge, and who have attained realization,
perceive them through the wisdom of realized vision.
To realize that the body and mind of sentient beings are the inconceivable Buddha-dharma is [the goal].
Question: For what reason do sentient beings neither know nor see this?
Answer: Because the wisdom that realizes and sees it is immovable.
Today, the body and mind of every sentient being are themselves the inconceivable Buddha-dharma;
they are themselves the worldly factors of the path (*loka-bhāga-mārga*).
Yet, ordinary people simply do not know this themselves.
Question: Why does Zhixiang state that the former two are "understanding through contemplation" (guanjie) and the latter two are "understanding through practice" (xingjie)?
"One sees the beginning and knows the end;
does one attain the beginning and realize the end?
Answer: "This merely refers to the process of cultivation."
If one speaks figuratively,

the cultivation of the *dhāraṇī* of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) of dependent origination throughout kalpas as numerous as the atoms in two Buddha-worlds constitutes "contemplative understanding" (*vipaśyanā*).
To realize and attain [this] in every thought-moment is the practice and understanding (*caryā-adhimukti*).
Regarding the "one who explains" and "discriminates within it," there are two types.
First, if we consider it from the perspective of the Buddha’s mind,
although there are no ten stages (bhūmis),
this is because the capacities of those he draws forth as his disciples are predominantly of the three vehicles (triyāna).
Vajragarbha was further addressed so that he might expound the Ten Grounds (*daśabhūmi*).
Desiring to enable Bodhisattvas on the stage of practice through faith (*śraddhācaryābhūmi*) to realize and enter the stage of wisdom (*jñānabhūmi*),
[the Buddha] subsequently employed a pen to delineate and reveal the Ten Grounds for the purpose of exposition.
Second, the Bodhisattva Vajragarbha, within meditative concentration, receives and articulates the discourse of post-meditative attainment;
this is what constitutes "teaching. It is because the Buddha takes non-discursiveness as his teaching that this [articulation] is the very basis of the teaching of non-discursiveness.
The designation "Vajragarbha" (Adamantine Treasury) is likewise ineffable,
yet it serves as the basis for relying upon verbal teachings.
As for "entering," it refers to those who, through faith and delight, attain realization.
The Buddha said:
"I have already cultivated and realized your body and mind.
You should know that there is nothing else different."
"Why is it that we have not yet known this?
It is simply because we lack faith that we do not obtain it;
through faith, one is able to know."
It is essential that there be faith.
Therefore, because one is able to believe that one's own body and mind are the inconceivable Buddha-dharma, it is called "faith.
Because one does not abandon this faith and is able to maintain it constantly, it is called "delight" (ruci).
Because of such faith and aspiration, and because of personally realizing one's own body and mind,
it is said that "realization is attained.
As for the "ground of wisdom," this refers to the wisdom of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*).
Zhixiang and Master Yuan both consider this phrase to be the fundamental entry.
As for the question regarding the twenty phrases added:
are these words spoken at the time of the formal exposition?
Is this listed by the compiler of the sutra?
Answer: From the perspective of the text, it is the compiler;
from the perspective of the meaning, it is the actual teaching itself.
Question: If one speaks in terms of its meaning,
is that which constitutes correct speech subsumed under the Buddha’s vocal action (vākkarman) or his mental action (manaskarman)?
Answer: It is vocal karma (*vākkarman*).
Question: Since the Buddha is in meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he possesses no vocal karma; there is no teaching that he performs speech.
Why, then, do you speak of "vocal" [karma]?
The answer is that the arising of the teaching proceeds from vocal karma (*vākkarman*).
From what, then, does this teaching that has arisen originate?
Fundamentally, because it takes non-speaking as its root, it is mental karma (*manaskarman*).
If one considers the modes of teaching through manifested signs— such as emitting light, stroking the head, grasping the hand, or touching the eyes—
these are subsumed under bodily action (*kāyakarman*). However,
because the Buddha’s vocal action (*vākkarman*) is said to be coextensive with great space, [it is not limited in this way].
The teaching that arises is also termed "Great Emptiness" (Mahā-śūnyatā).
As for "inclusion":
because the Dharma suddenly manifests within the mind that hears and believes in the inconceivable Dharma, it is called "inclusion."
Because the mind accords with the Dharma, it is called "entry.
Regarding the statement that "within wisdom born of hearing, all roots of goodness are subsumed," the Buddha’s Tripiṭaka says:

To hear and embrace the principles of the Perfect Teaching (Enkyō) in accordance with its essence, and for that hearing and wisdom to correspond with the principle—that is what is truly precious. Regarding the phrase "in accordance with its essence" (*shōtai*):
it refers to being in accord with the essence of the Ocean Seal Samādhi (*kaigimpon*).
For example, just as all sprouts depend upon the great earth,
so too there are no roots of goodness— whether mundane or supramundane— that do not arise in dependence on the Ocean Seal Samādhi,
nor do they abide without depending on the Ocean Seal Samādhi.
This Dharma of the Ocean Seal manifests instantaneously and with perfect clarity within the mind of one who possesses faith;
therefore, it is said that all roots of goodness are subsumed within the wisdom of hearing.
As for "entering through contemplation":
That which is heard through the wisdom of hearing is not lost through reflection.
Regarding "deliberation":
it concerns the dharmas contemplated within the wisdom of reflection.
One contemplates and discerns its characteristics through mental discourse.
"Entering" is as described above.
Regarding "all factors of enlightenment":
This is an inconceivable dharma.
As for "wisdom and skillful means":
when hearing the Dharma, the mind does not take external objects as its focal point.
To continuously contemplate this very dharma exclusively is the method.
It is because of this that [the result arises].
The mind then becomes inclined toward the Dharma;
this is its facility.
As for "discriminating and selecting":
His mind engages with the teachings he has heard,
distinguishing between what is contrary and what is concordant; it is because of this that [he attains such realization].
To adopt that which accords with the Dharma is selection;
to discard that which opposes the Dharma is rejection.
This is discernment. As for the mutual entry of dharmas and their characteristics,
it is because the dharmas that are contemplated appear within the mind, manifesting with perfect clarity and distinctness.
"Those various meanings" refers to the fact that the inconceivable dharmas are not singular.
"Immeasurable and manifold knowledge" refers to...
Since everything encountered and faced is nothing other than the inconceivable Buddha-dharma,
the dharmas that are known are limitless,
and the wisdom that knows them is likewise limitless.
Those who enter by means of transformation first enter through "comprehension," wherein they hear the inconceivable Dharma.
In the entry of "contemplation," they reflect upon and examine the characteristics of that Dharma.
In the entry of "the characteristics of phenomena," that inconceivable Dharma manifests within their minds.
When a bodhisattva first makes their vow,
it is not for the sake of saving themselves first;
rather, they desire to save others first.
Because he teaches all sentient beings by means of the dharmas manifested by his own mind,
it is called "entering through transformation.
He is one who possesses the complete names and phrases according to what is contemplated and deliberated, and who is skilled in preaching the Dharma.
Because one teaches and transforms sentient beings by means of the wisdom of reflection upon the dharmas that are reflected upon,
it is called "according with what is contemplated.
Because one establishes the name of teaching and transforming based on the dharmas heard through the wisdom of hearing as previously mentioned, it is so designated.
This refers to the perfection of names and terms.
Regarding "teaching with excellent determination":
if one teaches others by means of the Dharma heard from tradition.
This would not be a well-determined teaching.
For example, it is like clearly seeing a pearl in the palm of one's hand;
the mind’s clear comprehension of phenomena is likewise so.
Because one expounds for others the Dharma thus attained by oneself,
it is called "well-determined exposition.
As for "realization and entry":
This is because when one transforms sentient beings by means of the Dharma attained for oneself,
one's own practice is thereby fulfilled.
As for "all dharmas":
This is the inconceivable Dharma.
Regarding the "one with equal wisdom":
when this bodhisattva’s mind attains that Dharma, [he realizes it].
That mind and the dharma cannot be distinguished from one another.
It is like using a vessel to scoop up water from a full pond and pouring it back into that same pond.
One cannot distinguish that "this is the water of a vessel" or "this is the water of a pond";
therefore, it is called the Wisdom of Equality.
To transform and teach sentient beings is precisely to accomplish the Buddha-dharma for oneself.
Question: Why is it that the explanation of the entry into conversion (*vinaya-praveśa*) occurs only after the entry into realization (*praveśa-sākṣātkriyā*)?
Answer: It is because at the time of realizing the entry, one manifests the meaning that benefiting others is itself one's own benefit (*svārtha*).
This means that while a bodhisattva makes a vow solely desiring to deliver others,
at the time of delivering them,
it is the natural law (dharmatā) that they personally realize true suchness (tathatā).
The subsequent section on "attaining entry" explains the entry through teaching and transformation.
Regarding the entry through non-negligence:
it is like when one takes a pillar as an object of focus.
If the mind undergoes any shift,
that is precisely "letting go.
It is because of this letting go that [the mind wanders].
To incline toward other objects is precisely negligence.
In this way, the bodhisattva’s mind does not waver by relying on the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
Furthermore, the mind does not incline toward the objects of others;
hence it is said that one enters with heedfulness (*apramāda*).
As for the statement that "no demonic dharmas can defile [it]," it means:
There are four kinds of Māras:
first, the celestial; second, the person; third, the aggregates; and fourth, the afflictions.
Regarding the Māra of afflictions:
The three poisons are the roots from which afflictions arise;
that is to say, when the mind of a practitioner encounters adverse or favorable conditions,
it either gives rise to anger or greed.
That which cannot be stilled is the māra of afflictions (kleśamāra).
As for the māra of the aggregates (skandhamāra):
Among the five aggregates,
four are mind and one is form.
At the time of practice,
the mind that greedily seeks clothing, food, and so forth, as well as the objects of the five sensory realms,
is the Mara of Form (rūpamāra) and the mind of greedy seeking.
This is the demon of the mind.
As for the demon of persons:
it arises at the time of spiritual practice.
Parents, donors, evil friends, those who lust after beauty,
and the like are all human māras.
As for the celestial māra:
At the time of his practice, the sixth celestial Māra reflects to himself:
"This person has given rise to a superior mind and is cultivating superior practices;
he will surely attain a superior fruit."
They are not my followers;
therefore, they do not leave this person, constantly desiring to harass and disturb them.
If they are unable to harass and disturb them, [they will seek other means].
They immediately seek to cause his death;
these are the celestial Māras.
As for "entering progressively from stage to stage":
Although one can practice by inclining toward the signless prior to the seventh stage,
because this is still a stage involving effortful application,
one still gives rise to applied attention (*prayogamanasikāra*).
Having cultivated the stages from the eighth ground upward by means of the power of one’s own mental activity,
because the wisdom of signless contemplation has been manifested to its ultimate extent,
one proceeds by means of the power of one’s original vows and the power of the Dharma.
Because one practices with spontaneous ease,
it is called "transferring from stage to stage.
Regarding the purification of the roots of goodness such as non-attachment:
Because within the inconceivable Dharma there is fundamentally no threefold poison,
virtues such as non-attachment have existed since beginningless time; however,
this is explained by way of their provisional stations.
Thus, because the mind that clings to effortful application has not been relinquished prior to the seventh bhūmi,
the meaning of the purification of the three types of roots of goodness cannot manifest.
Upon reaching the eighth bhūmi, the stage of spontaneity, the meaning of the purification of the three types of roots of goodness is fully manifested.
It is said that this refers to the purity of the wholesome roots such as non-attachment.
Furthermore, the phrase "there are also wholesome roots and so forth" serves to decisively dispel doubt.
Within the ten stages (*bhūmi*),
each stage possesses both the roots of goodness of preparatory application (*prayoga-kuśalamūla*) prior to the stage,
as well as the roots of goodness belonging to the stage itself.
Regarding the preparatory practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*), it is said:
"Furthermore, there are roots of goodness. Regarding the roots of goodness on the actual stages, [it is said]: "Furthermore, there are roots of goodness."
This, then, is the inconceivable Buddha-dharma.
A doubt arises:
do the roots of goodness of the preparatory stages prior to the seventh stage give rise to the roots of goodness from the eighth stage upward?
To resolve this doubt,
it is said that the roots of goodness of the preparatory stage (*prayoga*) of the eighth ground give rise to the roots of goodness of that eighth ground itself. Therefore,
it is said that there are further roots of goodness capable of serving as the cause for the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*) of the supramundane path.
For the Bodhisattva who has fully entered into the secret wisdom of the Tathāgata,
with respect to the inconceivable Buddha-dharmas,
there are indeed no ten stages.
However, according to the various stations [of practice], it is provisionally divided into ten kinds of secret wisdom (*guhyajñāna*).
Since this secret wisdom is an inconceivable dharma,
it is said that by attaining this dharma, one enters the secret wisdom of all Tathāgatas.

The Buddha completely enters therein; as for "the one who enters the knowledge of all-knowledge," "all-knowledge" refers to the Buddha’s all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and all-aspect knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*).
As for "the one who enters knowledge":
This is the wisdom of the bodhisattva.
Because one enters the perfect wisdom of the Buddha by means of the bodhisattva’s wisdom,
the wisdom of the bodhisattva also becomes perfect wisdom.
Question: Regarding the "exhaustive entry" of a bodhisattva, it is said they "enter the secret wisdom of the Tathāgata";
regarding the "exhaustive entry" of a Buddha, it is said they "enter the all-encompassing wisdom of a Buddha. What is the difference between these two?
Answer: Bodhisattvas, having fully entered therein, attain inconceivable Buddha-dharma;
yet this is merely the causal stage for the fruit of fullness.
Buddhas, having fully entered therein, attain inconceivable dharma.
This is the fruit-stage of the exhaustion of causes;
therefore, it is treated separately.
Question: Master Huiyuan maintains that the Buddha’s entry into the state of exhaustion occurs while still within the stage of the cause.
What is the difference between this and the "exhaustive entry" (*kṣayapraveśa*) of a bodhisattva?
Answer: In terms of formal establishment (*vyavasthāna*), the exhaustive entry of a bodhisattva is established as the tenth stage (*daśamī bhūmi*).
The Buddha has fully entered and established himself in the stage of Buddhahood;
yet, the "fullness of the Buddha" is considered the fruit within the cause because bodhisattvas on the stages of practice through faith attain inconceivable Buddha-dharmas.
This is because one considers the fruit to exist within the cause;
thus, it is said that one attains the virtues of the Buddha-fruit,
but this does not mean that the Buddha is entirely present within the cause.

Regarding the phrase "these various bases (*āyatana*) are compared as equals," the meaning of Master Yuǎn [Huiyuan] is that the comparison extends from these various bases up to their differentiation as the objects of comparison.
That which is measured by progressing from the various *āyatanas* to increasingly superior stages is the intention of the Master of the *Piṭaka*.
The intention of Master Yuan, however,
is that it refers to the successive and progressively superior positions of the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages (*daśa-bhūmi*).
Because it is that which is entrusted, it is that which is discarded.

because within the One Vehicle there is no fixed distinction between beginning and end,
one [aspect] is raised as the primary principle.
The remainder serve as their companions.
Therefore, among the ten bases (*āyatana*), whichever one is raised is taken as the primary,
while the others are considered secondary.
One interpretation states:
The root is inherently constant as the root,
and the branches are inherently constant as the branches, yet they are without obstruction.
This means that entering exclusively by way of the fundamental [entrance] is called "comprehensive," whereas entering by way of the other nine entrances is not called comprehensive.
Entering exclusively by way of the other nine entrances is called "particular."
It is not that the names "root" and "entry" are distinct from one another.
Question: If this is so, how is it established that the root and the branches are without obstruction?
Answer: It is when, based on the general, the specific is opened up.
If one breaks down the general [categories] into nine specific ones,
then the specific obstructs the general;
when the specific is integrated to form the general, it is likewise so.
Thus, the general obstructs the particular; yet,
the general remains unmoved while forming the particular,
and the particular remains unmoved while forming the general.
The root is eternally the root;
the branches are eternally the branches;
yet they are able to achieve non-obstruction.
The "Chapter on the Six Characteristics" asks:
"The rafter is itself the house;
therefore, it is called the universal characteristic."
Since the rafters are themselves the hall, they are called "distinct characteristics" (viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa).
Based on this passage,
it can be admitted that the fundamental [cause] may in turn become the derivative [effect].
Question: Does the end return to become the beginning?
Answer: Within the One Vehicle, if it were not yet accomplished, then once it is accomplished, it is free from both beginning and end.
Although it is said that the rafters are themselves the house,
since they constitute the house, they are devoid of beginning and end; thus,
it is not the case that there were distinct rafters existing beforehand which later became the house.
Therefore, it is not said that the root returns to become the branch, nor that the branch returns to become the root.
Question: A rafter is a distinct condition;
yet you have already stated that the rafter is itself the house.
Therefore, since there is also the sense that the specific [categories] such as "inclusion" (saṃgraha) serve as the general [principle],
one might also say it has the sense that "the branches return to the root. Why should this not be so?
Answer: If the inclusion of the *samanta* (comprehensive) and so forth constitutes the general meaning, then it is the fundamental *āyatana* itself.
It is designated as "general" by virtue of its general name alone;
it is not designated as "general" by virtue of its specific names.
Therefore, if the "comprehensive inclusion" (saṃgraha) and so forth are treated as general categories,
they are simply referred to as the "fundamental bases" (mūlāyatana).
An ancient record states:
Within the fundamental entry into the Great Void, there are eight difficulties.
If one can understand these eight difficulties,
then even though one does not see their fundamental commentary, [the meaning will be clear].
This may be called knowing the subtle purport of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
If one does not know these eight difficulties,
then even if one obtains ten, twenty, or more commentaries, [one will remain ignorant].
One cannot say that this understands the purport of the *Dilun* (Treatise on the Stages).
It means that although within this great void there are no characteristics of totality or particularity,
there exists the sense in which totality and particularity can be distinguished.
This is difficult to perceive;
that is to say, it refers to perceiving the first three of the five layers, both collectively and individually.
Second, although within this great void there are no various teachings, practices, or stages,
yet there exist various teachings, practices, and stages that can be differentiated;
these, too, are difficult to perceive.
This is seen in the three vehicles and nine entrances of the outflows.
Within this great void, although there is neither permanence nor impermanence,
there is nevertheless the wisdom of permanence that eliminates obstacles and the wisdom of impermanence that eliminates obstacles.
It is also difficult to perceive.
This can be seen from the textual passages concerning the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and so forth.
If one considers it according to the thematic sections (*parivarta*), [it is as follows].
These are the two wisdoms— differentiation and equality— which arise from the cultivation of the causal and resultant stages and are innate.
Fourth, the wisdom of the permanent and the impermanent within this great void combines to form a single untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
It is also difficult to perceive.
This refers to the fact that the forty classes of dharmas and the assemblies of spiritual multitudes at the first gathering constitute the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*),
whereas Samantabhadra, Mañjuśrī, and the assembly of those born together with the Buddha constitute the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
This synthesis of the conditioned and the unconditioned constitutes the Dharmakāya,
the intrinsic wisdom of Vairocana. Within this great void,
there exists both that which arises and ceases, and that which neither arises nor ceases.
The synthesized essence of the Dharma-body is likewise difficult to perceive;
within this distinct teaching of non-abiding, there is no arising or ceasing through the three contemplations of shallow or deep levels.
Within the section on realization, there is the non-arising and non-ceasing of the Buddha-dharma.
Sixth, within this great void, the unmoving fundamental ignorance is itself the fully perfected essence of reality.
It is likewise difficult to perceive.
Within the fundamental and derivative aspects of ignorance according to the Final Teaching (Jōgyō), one perceives them by means of the seal of the letter *Pu* (*Pūrvā*),
thereby fixing them in their true nature.
Seventh, within this great void, it is difficult to perceive even the initial arousal of the mind that enters into the Buddhas,
nor the attainment of Buddhahood at the stage of total integration.
These various *āyatanas* are used as a basis for comparison;
this is seen in the passage concerning the distinctions in the meaning of wisdom (*jñāna*).
8. Within this great void, there is no station of hell for those who have resolved their minds [on enlightenment].
However, there are those who attain Buddhahood by generating the aspiration for enlightenment while in the midst of hell;
this is likewise difficult to perceive.
One should understand that this is seen in the texts through interpretation based on such scriptural statements.
Regarding the statement that "all dharmas are distinct up to the merits of the various stages," the *Dharmalakṣaṇa-śāstra* says:
"All dharmas are distinct because they abide in their own suchness; thus, one suchness is many suchnesses, and the characteristic of suchness is ungraspable."
Because it approximates fifty-four corners,
it is said to be suchness (tathatā) that cannot be divided;
this is the first corner of suchness.
This is because the second corner is equal [to the others] in its nature;
thus, the characteristics [of a distinct corner] cannot be apprehended.
When one considers a single corner, it is simultaneously considering all fifty-four corners.
It is said to be "suchness" (*tathatā*). This also applies to the second aspect.

The response, "All dharmas are known only by the Buddha;
they are not within my domain," and so forth,

That is to say, as previously stated:
